newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION-Inside Canberra-PM breaks ranks on China.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Inside Canberra-PM breaks ranks on China.

text.p: (From the "Inside Canberra" newsletter)

It is difficult to believe, but all the journalists in John Howard's media caravan which accompanied him to China missed the big story -- the PM has broken ranks with the rest of the OECD which has insisted that trade relations be linked to China improving her human rights record.
The result is bad news for industry.
Australia has until now regarded China as a non-market economy when it came to deciding dumping cases.
In the Great Hall of the People in Beijing on March 31, Howard explained to the Chinese Premier, Li Peng, that in future Australia would regard China as an economy in transition.

If China could show a good against which a dumping claim had been made in Australia was not subject to price control, or state subsidised, then Australian Customs would take the Chinese domestic price as the marker for dumping purposes.
The Australian Prime Minister apparently placed no conditions on this concession, certainly not in the area of human rights.
Indeed as we learned this week he did not even make as a condition that China should agree to the very mild initiative of annual human rights dialogue between the two countries.
To the surprise of the government, China this week announced its agreement.
And of course, Australia will not continue to annoy the Chinese by sponsoring the annual UN resolution calling on China to improve her human rights.
As far as we can discover the Prime Minister did not receive any trade quid pro quo in return for so pleasing China on dumping.
The PM's office told us Li Peng was "satisfied" with John Howard's explanation of the new dumping arrangements.
Why wouldn't he be?

As we first explained on November 22 last year, Trade Minister Tim Fischer, visiting Beijing in August last year, told his counterpart, Madame Wu Yin, that Australia was reviewing its policy on dumping.

The policy was, then, based on China being regarded as a non-market economy and when a dumping action arose, the Chinese domestic price was not taken as the yardstick, but rather the domestic price in a surrogate free market economy, such as Thailand, was used as the marker.

But later, to the horror of industry, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade advised Customs in the glyphosate acid dumping case brought by Monsanto to go off to China and discover the domestic price.
Subsequently, Monsanto lost the case. Industry was then, and still is, absolutely terrified of Chinese competition.
She produces a vast range of products (many receiving a subsidy of one form or another) at far below the Australian price and if she gets a dumping edge, then it would be a disaster.
For example the domestic price of Chinese peaches is around 40 cents and she could thus land peaches in Australia at 45 cents, still a dollar or more below the Australian domestic price.
If the Chinese domestic price was the measure, rather than a surrogate country's domestic price, there would be no dumping shown.
Further, other countries could dump peaches on the Australian market at, say, 85 cents.
As long as they were above the non-dumped Chinese price of 45 cents a can no dumping action would be taken against them because China would have set the dumping "floor".
In March Geoff Prosser, who is responsible for Customs, announced Cabinet had decided that China would henceforth be considered an economy in transition.
Most of the media failed to see the significance of this and it passed almost unnoticed.

However, industry was nervous and was entitled to be even more nervous when it received a discussion paper -- "China's Transitional Market -- Between Plan and Market" -- produced by the East Asia Analytical Unit of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.
A reading of the discussion paper would suggest that a majority of Chinese exported goods would no longer be regarded as belonging to a non-market economy.

For example, the discussion paper says that "for the purposes of the Customs Act, China can no longer be regarded as an economy in which the Government substantially influence the domestic prices of goods or substantially monopolises international trade".
And the study quoted the Chinese Ministry of Internal Trade as saying that by 1994 90 per cent of retail prices were determined by the market.
The Prime Minister's office told us this week that under the new arrangements it would be up to the Chinese to demonstrate its domestic price was a market price.
(But how does the Australian complainant or Customs contest this?)
The PM's office claimed industry was happy with the new arrangements.

True, it is happy the Government has agreed to treat each Chinese dumping case on its merits and legislation will be required to do this, otherwise the glyphosate precedent would have meant the Chinese domestic price would have to be the reference price in all dumping cases.
But from our soundings industry is bitterly disappointed that the glyphosate precedent was ever allowed to happen in the first place.
Interestingly when John Howard gave a press conference immediately after his meeting with Li Peng he did not volunteer anything of his discussions on dumping, nor did any journalist ask him.

We asked the Prime Minister's office this week why he had broken ranks with OECD countries and the answer we got was that a decision had been made that it was in Australia's national interest not to tie the dumping issue to the human rights accord.
The decision had been made to act in Australia's interest.
Howard kept talking about acting in Australia's interest when in China but none of the journalists twigged to what it was all about.

The office of the European Union Delegation in Canberra has confirmed to us that it is European policy that China should not be regarded as a market economy until she joins the World Trade Organisation and that to gain membership of this body will mean negotiations on her human rights record.
The American position is similar, but tougher on trade as material we received from the American Embassy has confirmed.

Far from going soft on dumping the Washington position is that China cannot accede to the WTO unless agreeing to safeguard provisions allowing China's trade partners to impose temporary duties to protect their industries from a surge of Chinese imports.
So as far as Washington is concerned, never mind about dumping, if Chinese imports, dumped or otherwise, start to hurt, the U.S. will put up the shutters.
-- Inside Canberra 61-6 273-1600
